P^{2} = a^{3}.title: Kepler's third law in solar units
P^{2} = a^{3}.about: For bodies orbiting the Sun, with the period in years and the semi-major axis in astronomical units, the constants in T^{2} = 4π^{2}a^{3}/(GM) cancel to P^{2} = a^{3}. It turns a planet's distance into its year, or the reverse, with no constants at all.
assumptions: Orbits around the Sun (one solar mass); for another star multiply a^{3} by 1/M in solar masses
The orbiting body's mass is negligible next to the Sun's
a is the semi-major axis, the average of the nearest and farthest distances

example.problem: Mars orbits the Sun with a = 1.524 AU. How long is its year?

T^{2} = 4π^{2} a^{3}/(G (M_{1} + M_{2})).title: Kepler's third law for a binary: total mass
T^{2} = 4π^{2} a^{3}/(G (M_{1} + M_{2})).about: Two bodies orbit their common centre of mass, and the period and size of the relative orbit give their combined mass. This is how the masses of binary stars, and of exoplanet host stars, are measured. In solar units (years, AU, suns) it becomes M_{1} + M_{2} = a^{3}/P^{2}.
assumptions: Two-body Newtonian orbit, no other bodies pulling
a is the semi-major axis of the relative orbit (one star around the other), not of each star around the centre of mass
vars: semi-major axis of the relative orbit
related: around the Sun, years and AU
each star's share of the orbit, giving the mass ratio

example.problem: A visual binary has a relative orbit with a = 20 AU and a period of 50 years. What is the total mass in solar masses?
steps: In solar units M_{1} + M_{2} = a^{3}/P^{2}

r_{p} = a(1 − e), r_{a} = a(1 + e).title: Periapsis and apoapsis distances
r_{p} = a(1 − e), r_{a} = a(1 + e).about: The closest (periapsis) and farthest (apoapsis) distances of an elliptical orbit from the body at its focus; around the Sun they are perihelion and aphelion, around the Earth perigee and apogee. They average to a, and their difference is 2ae.
assumptions: Keplerian ellipse, 0 ≤ e < 1
Distances from the centre of the central body (subtract its radius for altitude)

example.problem: The Earth's orbit has a = 1.496 × 10^{8} km and e = 0.0167. Find its perihelion and aphelion distances.

m_{1} − m_{2} = −2.5 log_{10}(F_{1}/F_{2.title: Apparent magnitude scale (Pogson's relation)
m_{1} − m_{2} = −2.5 log_{10}(F_{1}/F_{2.about: Magnitudes compare brightnesses on a backwards logarithmic scale: a brighter star has a smaller (even negative) magnitude. A difference of 5 magnitudes is a factor of exactly 100 in flux, so 1 magnitude is a factor of 100^{1/5} ≈ 2.512.
assumptions: Both fluxes measured in the same band (V, B, …)
Larger magnitude means fainter; the minus sign is easy to drop
−2.5 log_{10}, not −2.5 ln, and not log base 2.5
vars: apparent magnitudes of the two objects

example.problem: Vega (m = 0.0) and Polaris (m = 2.0). How many times brighter is Vega?

L/L_{sun} = (M/M_{sun})^{3.5}.title: Mass–luminosity relation
L/L_{sun} = (M/M_{sun})^{3.5}.about: On the main sequence a star's luminosity rises steeply with its mass, roughly as the 3.5 power. A star twice the Sun's mass shines about 11 times as bright. The exponent runs from about 2.3 for small stars to about 4 for Sun-like ones and falls again for the most massive.
assumptions: Main-sequence (hydrogen-burning) stars only; giants and white dwarfs do not follow it
A rough power-law fit, good to a factor of about 2

example.problem: Roughly how luminous is a main-sequence star of 2 solar masses?

t ≈ 10^{10} yr (M/M_{sun})^{−2.5}.title: Main-sequence lifetime
t ≈ 10^{10} yr (M/M_{sun})^{−2.5}.about: A star's fuel grows with its mass M but it burns it at a rate set by its luminosity, L ∝ M^{3.5}, so its life on the main sequence goes as M/L ∝ M^{−2.5}. The Sun lasts about 10 billion years; a 10-solar-mass star only tens of millions.
assumptions: Main-sequence stars; uses the rough mass–luminosity law
Order-of-magnitude estimate
M in solar masses: the ratio, not kilograms

example.problem: Estimate the main-sequence lifetime of a 10-solar-mass star.

θ = D/d.title: Small-angle formula
θ = D/d.about: An object of size D at distance d spans an angle θ = D/d radians when the angle is small: the arc of a circle of radius d is dθ, and for a small angle the arc and the straight size are nearly equal. Given any two of size, distance and angle it gives the third. Multiply radians by 206 265 for arcseconds, or by 180/π for degrees.
assumptions: θ ≪ 1 rad (good to 1% below about 14°)
θ in radians, not degrees; D and d in the same unit
related: parallax distance, also a small angle

example.problem: The Moon is 3474 km across and 384 400 km away. What is its angular size?

t_{H} = 1/H_{0}.title: Hubble time
t_{H} = 1/H_{0}.about: If the universe had always expanded at today's rate, everything would have been together a time 1/H_{0} ago. With H_{0} ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc this is about 14 billion years, close to the measured age of 13.8 billion years.
assumptions: H_{0} must be converted to 1/s (1 Mpc = 3.086 × 10^{19} km) before inverting
A rough age only: the real expansion slowed and then sped up

example.problem: Taking H_{0} = 70 km/s/Mpc, find the Hubble time in years.

v = c z.title: Recession speed from redshift
v = c z.about: For a small redshift the Doppler formula gives the speed directly: a source receding at v stretches each wave by the fraction v/c, so z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c. Combined with Hubble's law v = H_{0}d it turns a measured redshift into a distance.
assumptions: z ≪ 1 (below about 0.1); larger z needs relativity and cosmology
Motion along the line of sight

example.problem: A galaxy has z = 0.01. Find its recession speed and, with H_{0} = 70 km/s/Mpc, its distance.

1 + z = λ_{obs}/λ_{emit}.title: Redshift as a stretch of wavelength
1 + z = λ_{obs}/λ_{emit}.about: Light's wavelength is stretched by the factor 1 + z between emission and observation. In cosmology this factor is also how much the universe has expanded since the light left: at z = 1 it was half its present size.
assumptions: λ_{emit} is the known rest (laboratory) wavelength of the line
Works for any z, unlike v = cz
Observed over emitted, not the reverse; z > 0 is a redshift
related: the same thing written as a shift

example.problem: The hydrogen-alpha line (656.3 nm at rest) is seen at 721.9 nm. Find z.

θ = 1.22 λ/D.title: Diffraction limit (Rayleigh criterion)
θ = 1.22 λ/D.about: The smallest angle a circular aperture can resolve: two points closer than this blur into one. Bigger mirrors and shorter wavelengths see finer detail. On the ground the atmosphere (seeing, about 1 arcsecond) usually limits a large telescope first.
assumptions: Circular aperture, perfect optics
θ in radians; λ and D in the same unit
Small angles

example.problem: What is the diffraction limit of an 8 m telescope at 550 nm, in arcseconds?

M = f_{o}/f_{e}.title: Telescope magnification
M = f_{o}/f_{e}.about: The angular magnification of a telescope is the objective's focal length over the eyepiece's. Swapping eyepieces changes it. Useful magnification tops out at about 2× per millimetre of aperture; beyond that the image only gets bigger and dimmer.
assumptions: Telescope focused at infinity
Both focal lengths in the same unit

example.problem: A telescope with a 1200 mm objective uses a 25 mm eyepiece. What is its magnification?

P_{1}/P_{2} = (D_{1}/D_{2})^{2}.title: Light-gathering power
P_{1}/P_{2} = (D_{1}/D_{2})^{2}.about: A telescope collects light in proportion to its aperture area, so the diameter ratio squared compares two instruments. Doubling the diameter gathers 4 times the light and shows stars 1.5 magnitudes fainter.
assumptions: Circular apertures; central obstructions ignored
Both diameters in the same unit (inches with inches)
Square the ratio: twice the diameter is 4 times the light, not 2

example.problem: How much more light does an 8-inch (203 mm) telescope gather than a dark-adapted 7 mm pupil?

tan(φ) = μ.title: Angle of friction (angle of repose)
tan(φ) = μ.about: A block on a slope starts to slide when the slope's angle reaches φ with tan φ = μ_s. The resultant of normal and friction force is then tilted φ from the normal.

example.problem: μ_s = 0.5. Steepest slope before sliding?

T_{2} = T_{1} e^{μβ}.title: Belt friction (capstan equation)
T_{2} = T_{1} e^{μβ}.about: A rope or belt wrapped over a fixed drum can hold a much larger tension T₂ on one side than T₁ on the other, growing exponentially with the wrap angle. T₂ is the tight side.
assumptions: Rope on the point of slipping; rope mass ignored; flat belt (a V-belt uses μ/sin(α/2))

example.problem: A rope wraps 1.5 turns round a post, μ = 0.3. Holding 100 N, what load can it hold?

x̄ = (∫ x dA)/(∫ dA).title: Centroid by integration
x̄ = (∫ x dA)/(∫ dA).about: The centroid is the area-weighted average position. Pick strips whose area is easy to write, then integrate.

example.problem: Centroid of the triangle under y = x from 0 to b?

k_{eq} = k_{1} + k_{2}.title: Springs in parallel
k_{eq} = k_{1} + k_{2}.about: Springs that stretch the same amount share the load, so their stiffnesses add.

example.problem: Two 500 N/m springs side by side.

1/k_{eq} = 1/k_{1} + 1/k_{2}.title: Springs in series
1/k_{eq} = 1/k_{1} + 1/k_{2}.about: Springs end to end carry the same force and their stretches add, so the combination is softer than either.

example.problem: 300 N/m in series with 600 N/m.

x = A e^{−ζω_{n}t} cos(ω_{d}t − φ).title: Underdamped free response
x = A e^{−ζω_{n}t} cos(ω_{d}t − φ).about: A damped system with ζ < 1 oscillates at ω_d inside a decaying envelope A e^{−ζω_n t}. A and φ come from the initial position and velocity.

example.problem: ζ = 0.1, ω_n = 10 rad/s. How long until the envelope halves?

ζ = δ/√(4π^{2} + δ^{2}).title: Damping ratio from the logarithmic decrement
ζ = δ/√(4π^{2} + δ^{2}).about: Measure two successive peaks of a free vibration, take δ = ln(x₁/x₂), and this gives ζ. For light damping ζ ≈ δ/(2π).

example.problem: Successive peaks are 10 mm and 6 mm.

m x′′ + c x′ + k x = F_{0} cos(ωt).title: Forced vibration equation
m x′′ + c x′ + k x = F_{0} cos(ωt).about: A mass-spring-damper driven by a harmonic force. The solution is the decaying free response plus a steady oscillation at the driving frequency ω.

example.problem: m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m, no damping, F₀ = 10 N at ω = 5 rad/s. Steady amplitude?

X = (F_{0}/k)/√((1 − r^{2})^{2} + (2ζr)^.title: Steady-state amplitude (magnification factor)
X = (F_{0}/k)/√((1 − r^{2})^{2} + (2ζr)^.about: The static deflection F₀/k times a magnification that peaks near resonance (r = 1) at about 1/(2ζ), and falls below 1 for r > √2.

example.problem: At resonance with ζ = 0.05, how many times the static deflection?

tan(φ) = 2ζr/(1 − r^{2}).title: Phase lag of forced vibration
tan(φ) = 2ζr/(1 − r^{2}).about: How far the response lags the force: near 0 below resonance, 90° at resonance, near 180° well above it.

TR = √(1 + (2ζr)^{2})/√((1 − r^{2})^{2}.title: Transmissibility (vibration isolation)
TR = √(1 + (2ζr)^{2})/√((1 − r^{2})^{2}.about: The share of a vibrating force passed through the mounts (or of base motion passed to the mass). Isolation needs r > √2: soft mounts, low natural frequency.

example.problem: A machine runs at r = 3 on mounts with ζ = 0.05.

Q̇ = k A (T_{1} − T_{2})/L.title: Steady conduction through a plane wall
Q̇ = k A (T_{1} − T_{2})/L.about: Fourier's law integrated across a flat wall of thickness L: heat flows from the hot face to the cold face at a rate set by the conductivity, the area and the thickness. Use it for walls, slabs, windows and insulation layers once temperatures have stopped changing.
assumptions: Steady state: the face temperatures do not change with time
One-dimensional flow through the thickness; edges and corners ignored
Constant k (use k at the mean temperature for large spans) and no heat generated inside
T_{1} and T_{2} are the surface temperatures, not the air temperatures; with air films add 1/(hA) resistances
vars: heat transfer rate through the wall
wall area normal to the heat flow
related: the same law as a thermal resistance
when air films or more layers are in series

example.problem: A brick wall (k = 0.72 W/(m·K)) is 0.20 m thick and 12 m^{2} in area. Its inside face is at 20 °C and its outside face at 0 °C. How much heat flows through it?

q″ = Q̇/A.title: Heat flux
q″ = Q̇/A.about: Heat flux is the heat transfer rate per unit area. Conduction and convection laws give it directly (q″ = −k dT/dx, q″ = hΔT), and it is the number to compare across surfaces of different size, such as a chip's cooling load or solar irradiance.
assumptions: Uniform flux over A; otherwise this is the average flux
A is the area the heat crosses, normal to the flow; for a pipe say whether it is the inner or outer surface

example.problem: 864 W is conducted through a 12 m^{2} brick wall. What is the heat flux?

R = ln(r_{2}/r_{1})/(2π k L).title: Thermal resistance of a cylinder (pipe) wall
R = ln(r_{2}/r_{1})/(2π k L).about: Conduction resistance for heat flowing radially outward through a pipe wall or a layer of pipe insulation. The log appears because the area the heat crosses grows with radius. Put it in series with the inside and outside film resistances to get the heat loss from a pipe.
assumptions: Steady, radial (one-dimensional) conduction; long cylinder so end effects are ignored
Constant k, no heat generated in the wall
Layers of different material add in series, each with its own radii
vars: conduction resistance of the cylindrical layer
related: outside film, with A = 2π r_{2} L

example.problem: Find the resistance of 1 m of pipe insulation (k = 0.04 W/(m·K)) running from r = 5 cm to r = 10 cm.

R = (1/r_{1} − 1/r_{2})/(4π k).title: Thermal resistance of a spherical shell
R = (1/r_{1} − 1/r_{2})/(4π k).about: Conduction resistance for heat flowing radially through a spherical layer, such as the insulation on a tank or a cryogenic vessel. The area 4πr^{2} grows outward, so the outer layers resist less than the inner ones; integrating dr/(4πkr^{2}) gives this. Add film resistances 1/(hA) in series for the whole path.
assumptions: Steady, radial conduction; constant k; no heat generated
r_{1} < r_{2}, both measured from the centre: radii, not diameters

example.problem: A spherical tank's insulation runs from r = 0.5 m to 0.6 m with k = 0.05 W/(m·K). Find its resistance.

r_{cr} = k/h.title: Critical radius of insulation
r_{cr} = k/h.about: Insulation on a thin pipe or wire adds outer surface area as well as conduction resistance. The total resistance ln(r/r_{1})/(2πkL) + 1/(2πrLh) is smallest at r = k/h, so below that radius more insulation increases heat loss; above it, it reduces it. For a sphere r_{cr} = 2k/h.
vars: critical outer radius of the insulation

example.problem: A 2 mm diameter electrical wire is coated with plastic (k = 0.15 W/(m·K)) in still air, h = 10 W/(m^{2}·K). Find the critical radius. Does a 3 mm coat help or hurt cooling?
steps: The wire plus a 3 mm coat has r = 4 mm < 15 mm
Below r_{cr} the coat increases heat loss, so it helps cool the wire
example.answer: r_{cr} = 1.5 cm; the coat increases heat loss

assumptions: Cylinder with constant h outside; h itself changes somewhat with r
Matters only for thin wires and small tubes; for ordinary pipes r_{cr} is a few millimetres and any insulation helps
Electrical wires exploit it: a thin plastic coat below r_{cr} sheds more heat than a bare wire
related: the outer film, which shrinks as A grows

α = k/(ρ c_{p}).title: Thermal diffusivity
α = k/(ρ c_{p}).about: How fast a temperature change spreads through a material: its ability to conduct heat over its ability to store it. Metals have high α and respond quickly; insulators and water have low α. It sets the time scale of transient conduction through the Fourier number αt/L².
assumptions: Constant properties (evaluate at the mean temperature)
Use c_{p} in J/(kg·K), not kJ/(kg·K), or α comes out 1000 times too small
related: depth heat penetrates in time t

example.problem: Find the thermal diffusivity of copper: k = 401 W/(m·K), ρ = 8933 kg/m^{3}, c_{p} = 385 J/(kg·K).

Fo = α t/L^{2}.title: Fourier number
Fo = α t/L^{2}.about: Dimensionless time for transient conduction. Heat diffuses a depth of about √(αt) in time t, so Fo = (√(αt)/L)^{2} compares that depth with the body's size: Fo ≪ 1 means only the surface has felt the change, Fo ≈ 1 means it has reached the centre. The one-term Heisler solutions need Fo > 0.2.
vars: time since the surface temperature changed

example.problem: A 4 cm thick steel slab (α = 1.2 × 10^{−5} m^{2}/s) is quenched on both faces. Find Fo after 60 s and say whether the one-term solution applies.
steps: Both faces cooled, so L = half-thickness = 0.02 m
Fo > 0.2, so the one-term series is accurate

assumptions: L is the half-thickness of a slab cooled on both faces (the full thickness if one face is insulated), r_{o} for a cylinder or sphere; using the whole thickness is the usual mistake
For the lumped model L = V/A instead, the same length as in Bi
Constant properties
related: the other number the transient charts need

m = √(h P/(k A_{c})).title: Fin parameter
m = √(h P/(k A_{c})).about: Sets how quickly a fin's temperature falls from base to tip: 1/m is the decay length. It goes into every fin formula through m L. A fin longer than about 3/m behaves as infinitely long, so extra length adds almost nothing.
assumptions: Straight fin of uniform cross-section
One-dimensional conduction along the fin (thin fin, small Biot number across it)
Constant k and h along the fin
related: Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}) tanh(m L)

example.problem: An aluminium pin fin (k = 200 W/(m·K)) is 5 mm in diameter in air with h = 25 W/(m^{2}·K). Find m.

Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}) tanh.title: Heat rate of a fin, insulated tip
Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}) tanh.about: Heat leaving a straight fin of uniform section whose tip loses little heat. The fin cools along its length, so each extra bit of length adds less: tanh(mL) saturates, and beyond mL ≈ 2.5 a longer fin adds under 1%. √(hPkA_{c}) is the heat rate of an infinitely long fin per kelvin at the base. Use the corrected length L_{c} = L + A_{c}/P to account for tip convection.

example.problem: An aluminium pin fin (k = 200 W/(m·K)), 5 mm across and 5 cm long, stands in air with h = 25 W/(m^{2}·K), its base 60 K above the air. Find its heat rate.
steps: Q̇ = 0.0393 × 60 × tanh(0.5) = 1.09 W (the bare base area would pass only 0.04 W)

assumptions: Steady, one-dimensional conduction along the fin (thin fin, Bi = h t/k ≪ 1)
Uniform h and k; constant cross-section
Adiabatic tip, or L replaced by L + A_{c}/P (L + D/4 for a pin)
P is the wetted perimeter and A_{c} the cross-section, not the surface area

η_{f} = tanh(m L)/(m L).title: Fin efficiency
η_{f} = tanh(m L)/(m L).about: The heat a fin actually transfers over the heat it would transfer if every point were at the base temperature. Long or poorly conducting fins have cold tips and low efficiency. Multiply by the ideal heat h A_{fin} (T_{b} − T_{∞}) to get the fin's heat rate.
assumptions: Straight fin of uniform section with an insulated (adiabatic) tip; use L_{c} = L + A_{c}/P for a convecting tip
Constant k and h

example.problem: A pin fin has m = 10 m^{−1} and is 5 cm long. Find its efficiency.

Gr = g β (T_{s} − T_{∞}) L^{3}/ν^{2}.title: Grashof number
Gr = g β (T_{s} − T_{∞}) L^{3}/ν^{2}.about: Buoyancy over viscous forces in natural convection. Warm fluid near a hot surface is lighter by βΔT and rises; viscosity resists. Gr plays the role Re^{2} plays in forced convection, and the correlations use Ra = Gr Pr. Flow on a vertical plate turns turbulent near Ra ≈ 10^{9}.
vars: volumetric expansion coefficient, 1/T for a gas

example.problem: A 0.5 m tall vertical plate at 340 K stands in air at 300 K (ν = 1.6 × 10^{−5} m^{2}/s at the film temperature). Find Gr and whether the flow is laminar (Pr = 0.71).

assumptions: For an ideal gas β = 1/T_{f} with T_{f} the film temperature (T_{s} + T_{∞})/2 in kelvin, never °C
Evaluate ν at the film temperature
L is the plate height for a vertical plate, D for a horizontal cylinder, area/perimeter for a horizontal plate

Ra = Gr Pr.title: Rayleigh number
Ra = Gr Pr.about: The number that natural-convection correlations use, Nu = C Ra^{n}: buoyancy driving the flow against viscosity and heat diffusion holding it back. On a vertical plate the flow turns turbulent near Ra ≈ 10^{9}.
assumptions: Fluid properties at the film temperature (T_{s} + T_{∞})/2
Length L as the correlation defines it (height for a vertical plate)
vars: Grashof number g β ΔT L^{3}/ν^{2}

example.problem: A vertical plate 0.5 m tall has Gr = 6.0 × 10^{8} in air (Pr = 0.71). Find Ra and whether the flow is laminar.

Nu = 3.66.title: Laminar pipe flow, constant wall temperature
Nu = 3.66.about: In fully developed laminar flow through a round tube whose wall is held at one temperature, the Nusselt number is the constant 3.66 whatever the flow speed. Solve h = 3.66 k/D for the convection coefficient.
assumptions: Laminar: Re < 2300
Fully developed flow and temperature profiles (far from the entrance)
Circular tube, uniform wall temperature
related: same tube with uniform heat flux instead

example.problem: Water (k = 0.6 W/(m·K)) flows slowly through a 1 cm tube with its wall held at a fixed temperature. Find h.

Nu = 4.36.title: Laminar pipe flow, constant heat flux
Nu = 4.36.about: With a uniform heat flux at the wall (electric heating, or a counterflow exchanger with equal capacity rates), fully developed laminar flow in a round tube has Nu = 4.36, a little higher than for a uniform wall temperature.
assumptions: Laminar: Re < 2300
Fully developed flow and temperature profiles
Circular tube, uniform wall heat flux
related: same tube with uniform wall temperature

example.problem: Oil (k = 0.14 W/(m·K)) flows in laminar flow through an electrically heated 2 cm tube. Find h.

Nu = 0.664 Re^{1/2} Pr^{1/3}.title: Laminar flat plate, average Nusselt number
Nu = 0.664 Re^{1/2} Pr^{1/3}.about: The average heat transfer coefficient over a flat plate of length L with a laminar boundary layer, flow parallel to the plate. Solve h = Nu k/L.
assumptions: Laminar over the whole plate: Re_{L} < 5 × 10^{5}
Constant plate temperature; properties at the film temperature
Gives the plate-average Nu; the local value at x is half as large (0.332)
vars: Reynolds number ρ v L/μ, with L the plate length

example.problem: Air (Pr = 0.71) flows along a plate with Re_{L} = 10^{5}. Find the average Nusselt number.

Nu = 0.037 Re^{4/5} Pr^{1/3}.title: Turbulent flat plate, average Nusselt number
Nu = 0.037 Re^{4/5} Pr^{1/3}.about: The average heat transfer over a flat plate when the boundary layer is turbulent from the leading edge (for example tripped by a rough edge). With a laminar start, subtract 871 to get Nu = (0.037 Re^{4/5} − 871) Pr^{1/3}.
assumptions: Turbulent from the leading edge: 5 × 10^{5} < Re_{L} < 10^{7}
Properties at the film temperature
vars: Reynolds number ρ v L/μ, with L the plate length

example.problem: Air (Pr = 0.71) flows along a plate with a tripped boundary layer at Re_{L} = 10^{6}. Find the average Nusselt number.

Q̇ = ṁ c_{p} (T_{out} − T_{in}).title: Energy balance on a flowing stream
Q̇ = ṁ c_{p} (T_{out} − T_{in}).about: The heat a fluid stream gains (or loses, when negative) from its mass flow rate and its temperature change. In a heat exchanger the hot stream's loss equals the cold stream's gain, which gives an unknown outlet temperature.
assumptions: Steady flow, no phase change
Constant c_{p}; kinetic and potential energy changes neglected
c_{p} in J/(kg·K), not kJ/(kg·K), with Q̇ in W
related: the exchanger that moves the heat

example.problem: 0.5 kg/s of water (c_{p} = 4180 J/(kg·K)) is heated from 20 °C to 60 °C. What heat rate does it absorb?

Q̇ = ṁ c_{p} (T_{out} − T_{in}).try: 0.5 kg/s * 4180 J/(kg K) * 40 K to kW

NTU = U A/C_{min}.title: Number of transfer units
NTU = U A/C_{min}.about: A heat exchanger's thermal size, its conductance UA, measured against the smaller stream's heat capacity rate. With the capacity ratio c = C_{min}/C_{max} it fixes the effectiveness, which is the effectiveness-NTU method for rating an exchanger without knowing outlet temperatures.
assumptions: U constant over the exchanger
C = ṁ c_{p} for each stream; C_{min} is the smaller
vars: smaller of the two ṁ c_{p}

example.problem: An exchanger has UA = 4000 W/K; the smaller stream has C_{min} = 2000 W/K. Find NTU.

Q̇_{max} = C_{min} (T_{h,in} − T_{c,in}).title: Maximum possible heat transfer in an exchanger
Q̇_{max} = C_{min} (T_{h,in} − T_{c,in}).about: The heat an infinitely long counterflow exchanger would pass: the stream with the smaller heat capacity rate changes temperature by the whole inlet difference. Real exchangers pass ε times this.
assumptions: Uses the inlet temperatures of both streams, not the outlets
C_{min} is the smaller ṁ c_{p}: only that stream can swing the whole inlet difference; using C_{max} would break the energy balance
Temperature differences are the same in K and °C
vars: smaller heat capacity rate ṁ c_{p}

example.problem: Oil enters at 150 °C and water at 30 °C; the smaller capacity rate is C_{min} = 2000 W/K. Find Q̇_{max}.

ε = Q̇/Q̇_{max}.title: Heat exchanger effectiveness
ε = Q̇/Q̇_{max}.about: The actual heat rate over the most any exchanger could pass between the same inlets. Knowing ε from NTU charts or formulas gives the heat and both outlet temperatures directly, without the trial and error of the LMTD method.
assumptions: Steady operation, no heat lost to the surroundings
Q̇_{max} uses C_{min}, never C_{max}; with C_{max} ε could exceed 1

example.problem: An exchanger passes 168 kW where Q̇_{max} = 240 kW. Find its effectiveness.

ε = (1 − e^{−NTU(1 − c)})/(1 − c e^{−NTU.title: Effectiveness of a counterflow exchanger
ε = (1 − e^{−NTU(1 − c)})/(1 − c e^{−NTU.about: Effectiveness of a counterflow exchanger from NTU and the capacity ratio c = C_{min}/C_{max}. Counterflow keeps a temperature difference along the whole length, so it reaches the highest ε of any arrangement for a given NTU. For c = 1 it becomes NTU/(1 + NTU); for c = 0 (a boiling or condensing stream) every arrangement gives 1 − e^{−NTU}.
vars: number of transfer units U A/C_{min}

example.problem: A counterflow oil cooler has UA = 4000 W/K, C_{oil} = 2000 W/K and C_{water} = 4000 W/K. Find its effectiveness.

assumptions: True counterflow; parallel flow and shell-and-tube exchangers have their own formulas, and using this one for them overestimates ε
Constant U and specific heats, no heat lost to surroundings
c must be C_{min}/C_{max} ≤ 1, not the other way round

E_{b} = σ T^{4}.title: Blackbody emissive power (Stefan–Boltzmann law)
E_{b} = σ T^{4}.about: A perfect emitter radiates σT^{4} watts per square metre of surface; a real surface emits εσT^{4}. The fourth power makes radiation dominate at high temperature: doubling T multiplies the emission by 16.
assumptions: T is absolute (kelvin)
Blackbody (ε = 1); a gray surface emits ε E_{b}

example.problem: Find the emissive power of a blackbody at 1000 K.

α + ρ + τ = 1.title: Absorbed, reflected and transmitted radiation
α + ρ + τ = 1.about: Radiation striking a surface is absorbed, reflected or transmitted, so the three fractions add to 1. Most solids are opaque (τ = 0), so α = 1 − ρ; with Kirchhoff's law (ε = α for a gray surface) this gives the emissivity from a reflectance.
assumptions: Fractions of the same incoming radiation (same wavelength band and direction, or totals)
Opaque body: τ = 0

example.problem: An opaque surface reflects 30% of the radiation on it. What is its absorptivity?

ε = α.title: Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation
ε = α.about: A surface emits as well as it absorbs: its emissivity equals its absorptivity at the same temperature and wavelength. For a gray, diffuse surface the totals are equal too, so one number ε serves for both.
assumptions: Gray, diffuse surface for the total values
Surface and incoming radiation at about the same temperature
related: net radiation, small gray body in large surroundings

example.problem: An opaque gray plate reflects 20% of the radiation on it. What is its emissivity?

A_{1} F_{12} = A_{2} F_{21}.title: View factor reciprocity
A_{1} F_{12} = A_{2} F_{21}.about: The view factor F_{12} is the share of radiation leaving surface 1 that strikes surface 2. Both products equal the same geometric integral over the two surfaces, so they are equal. Reciprocity gives the reverse view factor from the forward one, so only the easy one needs working out.
assumptions: Diffuse surfaces with uniform radiosity
View factors depend only on geometry, not on temperature or emissivity
A small surface inside a large one: F_{small→large} = 1, so F_{large→small} = A_{small}/A_{large}, not 1
related: radiation exchange the view factor enters

example.problem: A sphere of area 1 m^{2} sits inside a box of inner area 6 m^{2}, so F_{12} = 1. Find F_{21}.

Σ_{j} F_{ij} = 1.title: View factor summation rule
Σ_{j} F_{ij} = 1.about: All radiation leaving a surface in an enclosure lands on some surface of it, so its view factors add to 1. Include F_{ii}, which is zero for a flat or convex surface and positive for a concave one.
assumptions: Closed enclosure: every direction leaving i meets a surface; an open side counts as a surface (the sky or surroundings)
F_{ii} = 0 only for flat or convex surfaces; forgetting it for a concave one is the usual mistake
vars: view factor from surface i to surface j
related: reciprocity, used with this to fill in the rest

example.problem: A sphere (area 1 m^{2}) sits inside a box (inner area 6 m^{2}), and F_{21} = 0.167. What fraction of the box's radiation lands back on the box, F_{22}?

w = 100 × m_{part}/m_{total}.title: Mass percent (percent composition)
w = 100 × m_{part}/m_{total}.about: The share of a mixture's or compound's mass that one part makes up, in percent. For a compound use the element's mass in one mole (atomic mass × subscript) over the molar mass; for a solution, mass of solute over mass of solution.
assumptions: Both masses in the same unit
For a solution, m_{total} includes the solvent
Mass percent is not mole percent; convert with molar masses

example.problem: What percent of water's mass (H_{2}O, 18.02 g/mol) is oxygen (16.00 g/mol)?

x_{i} = n_{i}/n_{tot}.title: Mole fraction
x_{i} = n_{i}/n_{tot}.about: The moles of one component over the total moles of the mixture. Mole fractions add to 1 and are unitless. They give partial pressures (Dalton: P_{i} = x_{i}P) and vapour pressures over solutions (Raoult: P_{i} = x_{i}P_{i}°).
assumptions: n_{tot} counts every component, including the solvent
Moles, not masses: convert grams with n = m/M first

example.problem: A gas mixture holds 2.0 mol of N_{2} and 0.5 mol of O_{2}. Find the mole fraction of N_{2}.

ρ = P M/(R T).title: Density of an ideal gas
ρ = P M/(R T).about: The ideal gas law with n = m/M rearranged for density. Gas density rises with pressure and molar mass and falls with temperature. Solved for M, it finds an unknown gas's molar mass from a measured density.
assumptions: Ideal gas behaviour (low pressure, well above condensation)
SI units: P in Pa (not kPa or atm), M in kg/mol (not g/mol), R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T in K (not °C)
P is absolute pressure, not gauge

example.problem: Find the density of CO_{2} (M = 0.044 kg/mol) at 1 atm (101 325 Pa) and 298 K.

ΔH = Σ BE(broken) − Σ BE(formed).title: Enthalpy change from bond energies
ΔH = Σ BE(broken) − Σ BE(formed).about: Breaking bonds costs energy and forming them releases it, so a reaction's enthalpy change is roughly the bonds broken minus the bonds formed. It gives a quick estimate when formation enthalpies are not to hand; tabulated ΔH°_{f} values are more accurate.
assumptions: Gas-phase reaction (bond energies are for gases)
Average bond energies, so the answer is an estimate (often within 10–20 kJ)
vars: bond energy (bond enthalpy) of each bond

example.problem: Estimate ΔH for H_{2} + Cl_{2} → 2HCl with bond energies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243 and H–Cl 431 kJ/mol.

ΔS° = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants).title: Standard entropy change of a reaction
ΔS° = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants).about: The reaction's entropy change from tabulated standard molar entropies, each multiplied by its coefficient. Unlike formation enthalpies, elements have nonzero S°. Fewer moles of gas on the product side usually means ΔS° < 0.
assumptions: Standard state: 1 bar, usually 298 K
Multiply each S° by its stoichiometric coefficient
S° is in J/(mol·K) while ΔH° is in kJ/mol: convert before using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
vars: standard molar entropy of each species

ln(K_{2}/K_{1}) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T_{2} − 1/T.title: Van 't Hoff equation
ln(K_{2}/K_{1}) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T_{2} − 1/T.about: How an equilibrium constant changes with temperature. An endothermic reaction (ΔH° > 0) shifts toward products when heated; an exothermic one shifts back toward reactants. It is Le Chatelier's principle made quantitative.
assumptions: ΔH° roughly constant over the temperature range
T in kelvin; ΔH° in J/mol with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
vars: equilibrium constants at T_{1} and T_{2}

example.problem: A reaction has K = 10 at 300 K and ΔH° = +50 kJ/mol. Find K at 350 K.

c = k_{H} P.title: Henry's law: gas solubility
c = k_{H} P.about: The concentration of a gas dissolved in a liquid is proportional to that gas's partial pressure above it: double the pressure and twice as many molecules strike and enter the surface. It is why a soda fizzes when opened and why divers get the bends. Warmer liquids have smaller k_{H}, so hold less gas.
assumptions: Dilute solution; the gas does not react with the solvent
k_{H} is for that gas, solvent and temperature; its units must match c and P (some tables give the inverse, P = k_{H}c)
Use the gas's partial pressure, not the total

example.problem: CO_{2} has k_{H} = 0.034 mol/(L·atm) in water. What concentration dissolves under 2.5 atm of CO_{2}?

K_{a} = [H^{+}][A^{−}]/[HA].title: Acid dissociation constant
K_{a} = [H^{+}][A^{−}]/[HA].about: The equilibrium constant for HA ⇌ H^{+} + A^{−}. A larger K_{a} (smaller pK_{a} = −log_{10} K_{a}) means a stronger acid. From a measured pH of a known solution it gives K_{a}; from K_{a} it gives the pH.
assumptions: Equilibrium concentrations in mol/L, not initial ones; dilute, ideal solution
Water's own H^{+} negligible (pH below about 6)

example.problem: 0.10 M acetic acid has [H^{+}] = 1.33 × 10^{−3} M at equilibrium. Find K_{a}.

[H^{+}] ≈ √(K_{a} c).title: Weak acid pH shortcut
[H^{+}] ≈ √(K_{a} c).about: When a weak acid dissociates only slightly, x = [H^{+}] is small next to c, and K_{a} = x^{2}/(c − x) ≈ x^{2}/c gives [H^{+}] ≈ √(K_{a}c). Check afterwards that [H^{+}] is under 5% of c; if not, solve the quadratic.
assumptions: Weak acid with x ≪ c (the 5% rule)
Water's own H^{+} ignored
Monoprotic acid

example.problem: Find the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid (K_{a} = 1.8 × 10^{−5}).

ln(k) = ln(A) − E_{a}/(R T).title: Arrhenius plot
ln(k) = ln(A) − E_{a}/(R T).about: Taking logs of k = A e^{−E_{a}/(RT)} gives a straight line in 1/T. Plot ln k against 1/T: the slope is −E_{a}/R and the intercept ln A. Measuring k at several temperatures this way gives the activation energy.
assumptions: A and E_{a} constant over the temperature range
T in kelvin, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)
vars: rate constant (its unit depends on the reaction order; 1/s for first order)
pre-exponential (frequency) factor, same unit as k

example.problem: A plot of ln k against 1/T has slope −6000 K. Find the activation energy.

E° = (RT/(nF)) ln(K).title: Standard cell potential and the equilibrium constant
E° = (RT/(nF)) ln(K).about: From ΔG° = −nFE° = −RT ln K. A positive standard cell potential means K > 1, and even a volt or so means an enormous K. At 25 °C it becomes E° = (0.0592 V/n) log_{10} K.
assumptions: Standard conditions; T in kelvin
n is the number of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction

example.problem: The Daniell cell (Zn/Cu) has E° = 1.10 V with n = 2. Find K at 25 °C.

c = λ ν.title: Speed, wavelength and frequency of light
c = λ ν.about: All electromagnetic radiation travels at c in vacuum, so wavelength and frequency are inversely related: halve one, double the other. Use it to convert a spectral line's wavelength to frequency before E = hν.
assumptions: In vacuum (in a medium the speed is c/n and λ shortens, while ν stays the same)
Convert nm to m first: 500 nm = 500 × 10^{−9} m

example.problem: What is the frequency of 500 nm (green) light?

FC = V − N − B/2.title: Formal charge
FC = V − N − B/2.about: Bookkeeping charge on an atom in a Lewis structure: its valence electrons minus the electrons it owns there (all its lone-pair electrons and half of its bonding electrons). Formal charges add up to the ion's charge. The best structure keeps them near zero, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
assumptions: Count electrons, not pairs: a lone pair is 2 nonbonding electrons, a double bond 4 bonding electrons
vars: valence electrons of the free atom
bonding electrons shared by the atom
related: Σ FC = charge of the species

example.problem: Find the formal charge on nitrogen in NH_{4}^{+} (four N–H bonds, no lone pairs).

N_{t} = N_{0} λ^{t}.title: Geometric (discrete) population growth
N_{t} = N_{0} λ^{t}.about: For populations that breed in seasons, the size is multiplied by the same factor λ each time step. λ > 1 grows, λ < 1 declines, λ = 1 is steady. λ = e^{r} links it to continuous exponential growth.
assumptions: Constant λ: unlimited resources, no density dependence
Non-overlapping generations or a fixed census interval
λ is a ratio (1.1 means 10% growth), not the rate r; λ = e^{r}
vars: number of time steps (generations or years)

example.problem: A population of 200 animals grows with λ = 1.1 per year. How large is it after 5 years?

N = M C/R.title: Mark-recapture estimate (Lincoln–Petersen)
N = M C/R.about: Mark M animals and release them; later catch C, of which R carry marks. If marked animals mixed back in evenly, the marked share of the catch R/C equals the marked share of the population M/N, so N = MC/R.
assumptions: Closed population: no births, deaths or migration between samples
Marks are not lost and do not change behaviour or survival
Marked and unmarked animals are equally likely to be caught
vars: animals marked in the first sample
animals caught in the second sample
marked animals among the second sample

example.problem: 50 fish are marked and released. Later 40 are caught, 8 of them marked. Estimate the population.

dN/dt = r N − a N P.title: Lotka–Volterra: prey
dN/dt = r N − a N P.about: Prey grow exponentially without predators (rN) and are eaten at a rate proportional to predator–prey encounters (aNP). With the predator equation it gives endless cycles, the predators lagging the prey by a quarter cycle. Prey hold steady when the predator count is P = r/a.
assumptions: Prey grow without limit when predators are absent
Predators eat in proportion to encounters (no saturation)
Well-mixed populations, continuous time
vars: attack rate per predator per prey
related: dP/dt = b N P − m P

example.problem: Prey have r = 0.5 per year and attack rate a = 0.01 per predator per year. How many predators hold the prey population steady?

dP/dt = b N P − m P.title: Lotka–Volterra: predators
dP/dt = b N P − m P.about: Predators grow from the prey they eat (bNP) and die at a constant per-capita rate m. They hold steady when the prey level is N = m/b; with fewer prey they decline, with more they grow.
assumptions: Predators have no other food
Births proportional to prey eaten; constant death rate
Well-mixed populations, continuous time
related: dN/dt = r N − a N P
prey level where predators are steady

example.problem: Predators have b = 0.002 per prey per year and die at m = 0.4 per year. At what prey level do they hold steady?

NPP = GPP − R.title: Net primary productivity
NPP = GPP − R.about: The energy producers fix by photosynthesis (gross primary productivity) less what they burn in their own respiration. What is left builds plant biomass and is all that is available to herbivores and decomposers.
assumptions: GPP and R measured over the same area and time, in the same units
R is the producers' own respiration only, not that of animals or decomposers
related: how much of NPP reaches the next level

example.problem: A grassland fixes GPP = 20 000 kJ/m^{2}/yr and its plants respire 12 000 kJ/m^{2}/yr. Find NPP.

E = P_{n+1}/P_{n}.title: Trophic (ecological) efficiency
E = P_{n+1}/P_{n}.about: The share of one trophic level's production that becomes production at the next level up. It is typically about 10%, the rest lost to respiration, waste and uneaten material, which is why food chains rarely exceed four or five levels.
assumptions: Production of both levels over the same area and time
The 10% rule is a rough average (range about 5–20%)
vars: production at the next level up

example.problem: Producers make 10 000 kJ/m^{2}/yr. At 10% per step, how much reaches the third-level (secondary) consumers?

G = 2^{n}.title: Number of gamete types
G = 2^{n}.about: By independent assortment each heterozygous gene pair offers two alleles, so n heterozygous pairs give 2^{n} kinds of gametes. Squaring gives the number of possible fertilisation combinations (4^{n}); homozygous pairs add no variety.
assumptions: Genes on different chromosomes (unlinked) or far apart
Count only heterozygous gene pairs
related: genotypes in the offspring of a self-cross

example.problem: How many kinds of gametes can an AaBbCc individual make?

V_{max,app} = V_{max}/(1 + [I]/K_{i}).title: Noncompetitive inhibition
V_{max,app} = V_{max}/(1 + [I]/K_{i}).about: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds the enzyme away from its active site, taking a share of the enzyme out of action. V_{max} falls while K_{m} stays the same, and adding more substrate cannot overcome it. At [I] = K_{i} half the activity is lost.
assumptions: Pure noncompetitive inhibitor (binds enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex equally)
Michaelis–Menten kinetics; inhibitor binding at equilibrium

example.problem: An enzyme has V_{max} = 100 μmol/min. A noncompetitive inhibitor is added at [I] = K_{i}. What is the apparent V_{max}?

V_{m} = (RT/F) ln((P_{K}[K^{+}]_{o} + P_.title: Goldman (GHK) equation: resting membrane potential
V_{m} = (RT/F) ln((P_{K}[K^{+}]_{o} + P_.about: The membrane potential when several ions leak across at once, each weighted by how permeable the membrane is to it. Chloride's inside and outside concentrations are swapped because its charge is negative. With only one permeable ion it reduces to the Nernst equation. Only permeability ratios matter.
assumptions: Steady state with no net current
Monovalent ions; constant field across the membrane
T in kelvin: RT/F = 25.3 mV at 20 °C, 26.7 mV at 37 °C
vars: membrane potential, inside relative to outside
outside and inside concentrations of ion X

example.problem: A squid axon at 20 °C has P_{K} : P_{Na} : P_{Cl} = 1 : 0.04 : 0.45 and (out/in) K^{+} 20/400, Na^{+} 440/50, Cl^{−} 560/52 mM. Find the resting potential.

SA/V = 3/r.title: Surface area to volume ratio of a sphere
SA/V = 3/r.about: A sphere's surface 4πr^{2} over its volume (4/3)πr^{3}. The ratio falls as the cell grows, so a large cell has too little membrane to feed its volume by diffusion, which limits cell size and favours flattened or folded shapes.
assumptions: Spherical cell; other shapes have their own ratios (a cube of side a: 6/a)
The ratio has units of 1/length, so its value depends on the unit: 0.3 μm^{−1} = 3 × 10^{5} m^{−1}

example.problem: Compare the surface area to volume ratio of a bacterium (r = 1 μm) and an amoeba (r = 50 μm).
example.answer: 3 μm^{−1} vs 0.06 μm^{−1}: the bacterium has 50 times more membrane per volume

RQ = V_{CO_{2}}/V_{O_{2}}.title: Respiratory quotient
RQ = V_{CO_{2}}/V_{O_{2}}.about: The volume of CO_{2} produced over the volume of O_{2} consumed. Each fuel needs a different amount of oxygen per carbon: glucose (C_{6}H_{12}O_{6}) already carries oxygen, so RQ = 6/6 = 1, while fat is oxygen-poor and needs more O_{2}, RQ ≈ 0.7. A mixed diet gives about 0.8.
assumptions: Steady state, aerobic respiration
Both gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure

example.problem: An organism releases 200 mL of CO_{2} while using 250 mL of O_{2}. Find its RQ.

SV = EDV − ESV.title: Stroke volume
SV = EDV − ESV.about: The volume of blood each ventricle pumps per beat: its volume when full at the end of diastole minus what is left at the end of systole. Times heart rate it gives cardiac output.
assumptions: Volumes of the same ventricle in the same beat
Left and right stroke volumes match on average

example.problem: A left ventricle holds 120 mL when full and 50 mL after contracting. Find the stroke volume.

EF = SV/EDV.title: Ejection fraction
EF = SV/EDV.about: The share of the filled ventricle's blood ejected in each beat, a direct measure of how well it contracts. Normal is about 55–70%; below about 40% signals a weakened heart (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction).
assumptions: Left ventricle unless stated
Divide by the end-diastolic (full) volume, not the end-systolic one

example.problem: A ventricle has SV = 70 mL and EDV = 120 mL. Find its ejection fraction.

MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3.title: Mean arterial pressure from a cuff reading
MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3.about: The time-averaged pressure in the arteries over a heartbeat. At resting heart rates the heart spends about two thirds of each beat in diastole, so the mean sits a third of the way from the diastolic to the systolic pressure. Organs need a MAP above about 60–65 mmHg to stay perfused.
assumptions: Resting heart rate (at fast rates diastole shortens and the mean moves toward the midpoint)
Not the simple average (SBP + DBP)/2, which overstates it
related: the same pressure from flow and resistance

example.problem: A blood pressure reading is 120/80 mmHg. Estimate the mean arterial pressure.

CL = k V_{d}.title: Drug clearance
CL = k V_{d}.about: The volume of plasma cleared of a drug per unit time. The body removes a fixed fraction k of the drug each hour, and that fraction of V_{d} litres is the volume effectively wiped clean. At steady state the dosing rate equals CL × C_{ss}, which sets the maintenance dose.
assumptions: First-order (linear) elimination
One-compartment model
Match time units: k per hour gives CL in L/h

example.problem: A drug has k = 0.1 h^{−1} and V_{d} = 40 L. Find its clearance.

LD = C_{target} V_{d}.title: Loading dose
LD = C_{target} V_{d}.about: A first dose that fills the volume of distribution to the target plasma concentration at once, instead of waiting four or five half-lives for maintenance doses to build up. Used for drugs with long half-lives such as digoxin or amiodarone.
assumptions: Full bioavailability (IV); for oral dosing divide by the bioavailability F
One-compartment model, no drug already present
mg/L times L gives mg; V_{d} given in L/kg must be multiplied by body mass first

example.problem: A drug's target plasma level is 15 mg/L and its V_{d} = 35 L. What IV loading dose is needed?

M = I/A.title: Magnification
M = I/A.about: How many times larger an image (a drawing, photo or microscope view) is than the real object: image size over actual size. Rearranged, A = I/M gives the true size of a specimen from its image. Convert both sizes to the same unit first.
assumptions: Both sizes in the same unit (1 mm = 1000 μm)

example.problem: A cell 20 μm across is drawn 5 mm wide. What is the drawing's magnification?

C = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2.title: Mohr's circle: centre
C = (σ_{x} + σ_{y})/2.about: Plotting (σ, τ) on every plane through a point traces a circle whose centre is the average normal stress C and whose radius is R = √(((σ_{x} − σ_{y})/2)^{2} + τ_{xy}^{2}). The principal stresses are C ± R and the largest in-plane shear is R, acting where the normal stress is C.
assumptions: Plane stress (σ_{z} = τ_{xz} = τ_{yz} = 0)
Pure equilibrium: holds for any material
vars: centre of Mohr's circle (average normal stress)
shear stress (sets the radius with σ_{x} − σ_{y})

example.problem: At a point σ_{x} = 80 MPa, σ_{y} = −20 MPa and τ_{xy} = 40 MPa. Find the circle's centre and radius, the principal stresses and τ_{max}.

n = σ_{Y}/σ_{v}.title: Factor of safety against yield
n = σ_{Y}/σ_{v}.about: How many times the load could grow before the part starts to yield: the yield strength over the von Mises equivalent stress at the worst point. Designs typically need n of 1.5 to 3 depending on how well loads and materials are known. Tresca's version is n = σ_{Y}/(σ_{1} − σ_{3}).
assumptions: Ductile, isotropic material under static load
Stresses scale in proportion with the load (linear elastic)
vars: von Mises equivalent stress at the critical point
related: von Mises for a shaft surface

example.problem: A steel part with σ_{Y} = 250 MPa has a peak von Mises stress of 100 MPa. Find its factor of safety.

K_{t} = σ_{max}/σ_{nom}.title: Stress concentration factor
K_{t} = σ_{max}/σ_{nom}.about: Holes, notches, fillets and keyways raise the local peak stress above the nominal value P/A or Mc/I computed for the net section. K_{t} depends only on geometry and comes from charts; a small circular hole in a wide plate under tension gives K_{t} = 3.
assumptions: Linear elastic material; K_{t} is a geometric factor
Ductile parts under static load can often ignore it (local yielding redistributes stress); brittle parts and fatigue cannot

example.problem: A wide plate with a small circular hole carries a nominal tensile stress of 50 MPa. What is the peak stress at the hole's edge?
steps: K_{t} ≈ 3 for a small hole in a wide plate

U = P^{2}L/(2AE).title: Strain energy in an axially loaded bar
U = P^{2}L/(2AE).about: The elastic energy stored in a bar under axial load, the triangular area under its load–deflection line, (1/2)Pδ. Castigliano's theorem differentiates it: ∂U/∂P gives the deflection at the load, which is a quick route to deflections of trusses.
assumptions: Linear elastic material
P, A and E constant along L (otherwise sum segments)
Energy goes as P^{2}, so loads don't superpose: U for two loads together is not the sum of each alone
related: the same energy from the deflection

example.problem: A 1 m steel bar (E = 200 GPa) of 100 mm^{2} cross-section carries 10 kN. How much strain energy does it store?

q = VQ/I.title: Shear flow
q = VQ/I.about: Shear force per unit length along a beam: the horizontal force that the welds, nails or bolts joining built-up parts must carry. It comes from the change in bending stress along the beam: the flange's force differs from one section to the next by V dx·Q/I, and the joint must pass that difference. Fastener spacing is s = F/q for fasteners of capacity F each.
vars: first moment of the joined part about the neutral axis
second moment of the whole section

example.problem: A timber box beam carries V = 10 kN. Its flange has Q = 2 × 10^{−4} m^{3} and the section has I = 4 × 10^{−5} m^{4}. Find the shear flow and the nail spacing for nails good for 1 kN each (one row).

assumptions: Linear elastic beam, the same assumptions as τ = VQ/(It)
Q is the first moment about the neutral axis of only the part outside the joint (the flange being held on), not of half the section
Shared by all fasteners in a row: with n per row, s = nF/q
related: shear stress: q spread over thickness t

σ_{cr} = π^{2}E/(KL/r)^{2}.title: Critical buckling stress
σ_{cr} = π^{2}E/(KL/r)^{2}.about: Euler's buckling load divided by the area, written with the slenderness ratio KL/r. It shows that buckling depends on slenderness and stiffness, not strength. Valid only while σ_{cr} is below the proportional limit; stockier columns need Johnson's parabola.
assumptions: Slender, straight, linear elastic column with a centred load
Use the smallest radius of gyration r (weakest axis)
K: 1 pinned–pinned, 2 fixed–free, 0.7 fixed–pinned, 0.5 fixed–fixed

example.problem: A steel column (E = 200 GPa) has slenderness KL/r = 150. Find its critical buckling stress.
example.answer: σ_{cr} ≈ 87.7 MPa (below yield, so Euler applies)

r = √(I/A).title: Radius of gyration of a section
r = √(I/A).about: The distance from the axis at which the whole area could be concentrated to give the same second moment of area. It measures how well a section resists buckling per unit area; columns buckle about the axis with the smallest r.
assumptions: I about the same axis the column would buckle about (usually the weaker one)
For a wide-flange or rectangular section use r_{min}; the strong-axis r overestimates the buckling load

example.problem: Find the radius of gyration of a 50 mm by 50 mm square bar.

A_{1} v_{1} = A_{2} v_{2}.title: Continuity for incompressible flow
A_{1} v_{1} = A_{2} v_{2}.about: What flows into a pipe must flow out, so with constant density the volume flow rate Q = Av is the same at every section and the fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows. Use it with Bernoulli for nozzles and Venturi meters.
assumptions: Incompressible fluid (liquids; gases below about Mach 0.3)
Steady flow, one inlet and one outlet
v is the mean speed over each section

example.problem: Water flows at 2 m/s in a 10 cm pipe that narrows to 5 cm. How fast does it go in the narrow part?

v = √(2gh).title: Torricelli's law: outflow from a tank
v = √(2gh).about: Liquid leaves a hole a depth h below the free surface at the speed of a free fall from height h. It follows from Bernoulli between the surface and the jet. Real orifices give a little less speed and a contracted jet: multiply the ideal flow by a discharge coefficient of about 0.6 for a sharp-edged hole.
assumptions: Large tank: the surface falls slowly
No losses (inviscid); both surface and jet at atmospheric pressure
vars: depth of the hole below the surface
related: actual flow rate through the hole

example.problem: Water drains through a hole 2 m below the surface of a large tank. How fast is the jet?

F_{D} = (1/2) C_{D} ρ v^{2} A.title: Drag force
F_{D} = (1/2) C_{D} ρ v^{2} A.about: The force a fluid exerts on a body against its motion. (1/2)ρv^{2} is the dynamic pressure of the oncoming flow, and C_{D} says how much of it acts on the area: it packs in shape and Reynolds number. About 1.0–1.2 for a flat plate face-on, 0.47 for a sphere, 0.3 for a car, 0.04 for a streamlined body.
assumptions: C_{D} taken at the right Reynolds number and for the same reference area A (frontal for cars, planform for wings)
Steady flow; well away from walls and the free surface
v is relative to the fluid: add a headwind

example.problem: A car (C_{D} = 0.3, frontal area 2.2 m^{2}) drives at 30 m/s through air at 1.2 kg/m^{3}. Find the drag.

F_{L} = (1/2) C_{L} ρ v^{2} A.title: Lift force
F_{L} = (1/2) C_{L} ρ v^{2} A.about: The force on a wing perpendicular to the oncoming flow: dynamic pressure times planform area times the lift coefficient. C_{L} rises roughly linearly with angle of attack (about 0.1 per degree) until the wing stalls near C_{L} ≈ 1.2–1.6.
assumptions: C_{L} for this wing section and Reynolds number, below stall
A is the planform (wing) area, not the frontal area
related: stall speed for a weight W

example.problem: A wing of 16 m^{2} flies at 40 m/s in air of 1.2 kg/m^{3} with C_{L} = 1.2. How much lift does it make?

f = 64/Re.title: Laminar friction factor
f = 64/Re.about: For fully developed laminar flow in a round pipe the Darcy friction factor follows exactly from the Hagen–Poiseuille velocity profile and does not depend on roughness. Put it into Darcy–Weisbach for the head loss. Turbulent flow needs the Moody chart or Colebrook equation.
assumptions: Laminar: Re below about 2300
Fully developed flow in a circular pipe
Darcy (not Fanning) friction factor; Fanning is a quarter of it

example.problem: Oil flows in a round pipe at Re = 1000. Find the Darcy friction factor.

h_{m} = K v^{2}/(2g).title: Minor losses: fittings, valves and bends
h_{m} = K v^{2}/(2g).about: Head lost at fittings, valves, bends, entrances and exits, written as K velocity heads. Add them to the pipe-friction loss in the energy equation. Typical K: 90° elbow 0.3–0.9, open globe valve about 10, sharp entrance 0.5, exit into a tank 1.
assumptions: Turbulent flow (K is roughly constant there)
v is the mean speed in the pipe at the fitting (the smaller pipe for a contraction)
related: the same loss as a pressure drop

example.problem: Water flows at 3 m/s through an elbow with K = 0.9. What head is lost?

D_{h} = 4A/P_{w}.title: Hydraulic diameter
D_{h} = 4A/P_{w}.about: An equivalent diameter that lets round-pipe results (Reynolds number, friction factor, Nusselt correlations) serve ducts of other shapes. For a full circle it is just D.
assumptions: Turbulent flow in shapes not too far from round (laminar results for odd shapes need their own constants)
P_{w} counts only the wetted perimeter (the walls in contact with the fluid)
related: use it in the Reynolds number

example.problem: Find the hydraulic diameter of a 0.2 m by 0.1 m rectangular duct.

P = ρ g Q h.title: Pump (hydraulic) power
P = ρ g Q h.about: The power a pump gives the fluid to raise its head by h at a flow rate Q. Divide by the pump efficiency for the shaft power the motor must supply.
assumptions: h is the total head added (elevation plus friction and minor losses)
Steady flow, incompressible fluid
vars: hydraulic power given to the fluid
related: minor losses that add to h

example.problem: A pump lifts 0.05 m^{3}/s of water 20 m at 75% efficiency. Find the power to the water and the shaft power.
example.answer: P ≈ 9.81 kW to the water; shaft ≈ 13.1 kW

L_{c} = L + A_{c}/P.title: Corrected fin length for a convective tip
L_{c} = L + A_{c}/P.about: A fin whose tip loses heat by convection can be treated as an insulated-tip fin made slightly longer, by the tip area over the perimeter. Use L_{c} in place of L in the adiabatic-tip heat rate and efficiency. It is L + t/2 for a thin plate fin and L + D/4 for a pin fin.
assumptions: Same h on the tip as on the sides
Error under about 8% when h t/k (or h D/(2k)) is under 0.0625
related: Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}) tanh(m L)

example.problem: A pin fin 5 mm across and 40 mm long convects from its tip. What length goes in the adiabatic-tip formulas?

Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}).title: Heat rate of an infinitely long fin
Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}).about: A fin so long that its tip reaches the air temperature loses this much heat. It is the largest any fin of that section can pass, and it is the adiabatic-tip result with tanh(mL) → 1, close once m L > 2.65.
assumptions: Steady, one-dimensional conduction along the fin
Constant k and h
Long fin: m L above about 2.65
related: Q̇ = √(h P k A_{c}) (T_{b} − T_{∞}) tanh(m L)

example.problem: A long 5 mm copper rod (k = 400 W/(m·K)) sticks out of a 100 °C wall into 25 °C air with h = 25 W/(m^{2}·K). How much heat does it lose?

Q̇ = η_{f} h A_{f} (T_{b} − T_{∞}).title: Fin heat rate from its efficiency
Q̇ = η_{f} h A_{f} (T_{b} − T_{∞}).about: A fin passes its efficiency times the heat its whole surface would pass if it were all at the base temperature. Use it with an efficiency read from a chart or found from tanh(mL)/(mL), for fins of any shape.
assumptions: η_{f} for the same tip condition (use L_{c} for a convecting tip)
Constant h over the fin
vars: fin surface area exposed to the fluid

example.problem: A fin with 0.002 m^{2} of surface has an efficiency of 0.85, h = 40 W/(m^{2}·K), and its base is 60 K above the air. Find its heat rate.

ε_{fin} = Q̇_{fin}/(h A_{c} (T_{b} − T_{.title: Fin effectiveness
ε_{fin} = Q̇_{fin}/(h A_{c} (T_{b} − T_{.about: How much more heat a fin passes than the bare base area it covers would. A fin is worth adding only when its effectiveness is well above 1, usually above 2. High k, small h and thin, closely spaced fins help.
assumptions: Same h and temperatures with and without the fin

example.problem: The 5 mm copper rod that loses 4.17 W (h = 25 W/(m^{2}·K), 75 K above the air) covers 1.96×10^{−5} m^{2} of wall. What is its effectiveness?

T(x) = T_{s} + (q̇ L^{2}/(2k))(1 − x^{2}.title: Plane wall with uniform heat generation
T(x) = T_{s} + (q̇ L^{2}/(2k))(1 − x^{2}.about: A wall that makes heat inside (by electric current, nuclear or chemical reaction) has a parabolic temperature profile, hottest at the middle. The maximum, at x = 0, is T_{s} + q̇L^{2}/(2k). Each face passes q̇ L per unit area.
assumptions: Steady, one-dimensional, constant k
Both faces at T_{s}; x from the mid-plane, wall thickness 2L

example.problem: A 50 mm thick plate (k = 20 W/(m·K)) generates 10^{6} W/m^{3}, and both faces are held at 80 °C. What is the centre temperature?

T(r) = T_{s} + (q̇ r_{o}^{2}/(4k))(1 − r.title: Solid cylinder (wire) with heat generation
T(r) = T_{s} + (q̇ r_{o}^{2}/(4k))(1 − r.about: A rod or wire that generates heat throughout, as a current-carrying wire or a fuel rod does, is hottest on its axis, T_{s} + q̇r_{o}^{2}/(4k). For a wire, q̇ = I^{2}R/(volume).
assumptions: Steady, radial conduction only, constant k
Surface held at T_{s}

example.problem: A 2 mm diameter wire (k = 15 W/(m·K)) generates 2×10^{8} W/m^{3} with its surface at 60 °C. Find its centre temperature.

Nu = C Ra^{n}.title: Natural convection correlation
Nu = C Ra^{n}.about: In natural (free) convection the flow is driven by buoyancy, and the average Nusselt number follows a power of the Rayleigh number Ra = Gr Pr. For a vertical plate of height L, C = 0.59 and n = 1/4 when Ra is 10^{4} to 10^{9} (laminar), C = 0.10 and n = 1/3 above. Then h = Nu k/L.
assumptions: Properties at the film temperature (T_{s} + T_{∞})/2
C and n depend on the shape and the Ra range
vars: constants for the geometry and range

example.problem: A 0.5 m tall vertical plate in air has Ra = 5×10^{8}. Find Nu and h (k = 0.026 W/(m·K)).

(T_{s} − T_{out})/(T_{s} − T_{in}) = e^{.title: Pipe outlet temperature at constant wall temperature
(T_{s} − T_{out})/(T_{s} − T_{in}) = e^{.about: Fluid flowing through a pipe with its wall held at T_{s} approaches T_{s} exponentially along the length. Use it to find the outlet (mean) temperature, or the length needed to reach one. The heat gained is then ṁ c_{p} (T_{out} − T_{in}).
assumptions: Constant wall temperature and constant h
Mean (bulk) fluid temperatures

example.problem: Water (c_{p} = 4180 J/(kg·K)) at 0.05 kg/s enters a 3 m long, 20 mm pipe at 20 °C. The wall is at 100 °C and h = 500 W/(m^{2}·K). Find the outlet temperature.

ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,out}, ΔT_{2} =.title: End temperature differences: counterflow exchanger
ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,out}, ΔT_{2} =.about: In counterflow the hot inlet meets the cold outlet at one end and the hot outlet meets the cold inlet at the other. These two end differences go into the log mean temperature difference. Counterflow gives a larger LMTD, so a smaller area, than parallel flow.
assumptions: Steady flow, no heat lost to the surroundings
vars: temperature differences at the two ends

example.problem: Oil cools from 150 °C to 90 °C while water warms from 30 °C to 70 °C in counterflow. Find the LMTD.

ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,in}, ΔT_{2} =.title: End temperature differences: parallel-flow exchanger
ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,in}, ΔT_{2} =.about: In parallel flow both streams enter at the same end, so the inlets are compared at one end and the outlets at the other. The cold outlet can never pass the hot outlet.
assumptions: Steady flow, no heat lost to the surroundings
vars: temperature differences at the two ends
related: ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,out},  ΔT_{2} = T_{h,out} − T_{c,in}

example.problem: Oil cools from 150 °C to 90 °C while water warms from 30 °C to 70 °C in parallel flow. Find the LMTD.

Q̇ = U A F ΔT_{m,cf}.title: LMTD with a correction factor (shell-and-tube, cross-flow)
Q̇ = U A F ΔT_{m,cf}.about: For multipass shell-and-tube and cross-flow exchangers, work out the LMTD as if the exchanger were counterflow and multiply by a correction factor F (read from a chart; F = 1 for pure counterflow or when one stream changes phase).
assumptions: Steady flow, constant U
F from the chart for that exchanger, usually 0.75 to 1
related: ΔT_{1} = T_{h,in} − T_{c,out},  ΔT_{2} = T_{h,out} − T_{c,in}

example.problem: A shell-and-tube exchanger has U = 300 W/(m^{2}·K), A = 10 m^{2}, a counterflow LMTD of 69.5 K and F = 0.92. Find its heat rate.

ε = (1 − e^{−NTU(1 + c)})/(1 + c).title: Effectiveness of a parallel-flow exchanger
ε = (1 − e^{−NTU(1 + c)})/(1 + c).about: The ε-NTU relation for parallel flow. Use it when the outlet temperatures are unknown: find NTU and c, then ε, then Q̇ = ε C_{min} (T_{h,in} − T_{c,in}). It never exceeds 1/(1 + c), however large the exchanger.
assumptions: Steady flow, constant U and specific heats

example.problem: A parallel-flow exchanger has NTU = 1.5 and c = 0.5. Find its effectiveness.

ε = 1 − e^{−NTU}.title: Effectiveness when one stream boils or condenses
ε = 1 − e^{−NTU}.about: When one stream changes phase its temperature stays fixed, so C_{max} is effectively infinite and c = 0. Every exchanger type then has this same effectiveness.
assumptions: c = C_{min}/C_{max} = 0: a condenser or boiler

example.problem: A condenser has NTU = 2. What fraction of the maximum possible heat does it pass?

Q̇_{12} = σ (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4})/((1.title: Radiation between two gray surfaces (two-surface enclosure)
Q̇_{12} = σ (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4})/((1.about: The net radiation between two diffuse gray surfaces that see only each other, as a radiation network: two surface resistances and one space resistance in series. It covers concentric cylinders and spheres, parallel plates and a small body in a large room (where it reduces to ε σ A (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4})).
assumptions: Diffuse, gray, opaque surfaces at uniform temperatures
The two surfaces form an enclosure; non-participating medium between them
Temperatures in kelvin

example.problem: A 100 mm pipe at 500 K (ε = 0.8) runs inside a duct at 300 K (ε = 0.5) with 0.8 m^{2} of wall per metre. Find the radiation per metre of pipe.

q″ = σ (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4})/(1/ε_{1}.title: Radiation between large parallel plates
q″ = σ (T_{1}^{4} − T_{2}^{4})/(1/ε_{1}.about: The two-surface enclosure result for two large parallel plates, where A_{1} = A_{2} and F_{12} = 1. Per unit area. A thin radiation shield between them roughly halves it.
assumptions: Plates large next to their gap
Diffuse gray surfaces; temperatures in kelvin

example.problem: Two large plates at 600 K (ε = 0.7) and 400 K (ε = 0.4) face each other. Find the net radiation flux.

E = −G M m/(2a).title: Orbital energy
E = −G M m/(2a).about: The total (kinetic plus potential) energy of a body on a bound orbit depends only on the semi-major axis a. It is negative; a less negative energy means a bigger orbit, and zero means just escaping. The energy to raise an orbit is the difference between two of these.
assumptions: Two bodies, m much smaller than M
Bound (elliptical or circular) orbit; a = r for a circle

example.problem: A 1000 kg satellite circles Earth (GM = 3.986×10^{14} m^{3}/s^{2}) at a = 7000 km. What is its orbital energy?

1/S = 1/P_{1} − 1/P_{2}.title: Synodic period
1/S = 1/P_{1} − 1/P_{2}.about: The time between successive alignments of two orbiting bodies as seen from one of them, such as Mars returning to opposition as seen from Earth. P_{1} is the shorter (inner) period, P_{2} the longer.
assumptions: Circular, coplanar orbits in the same direction
vars: sidereal period of the inner (faster) body
sidereal period of the outer body
related: Kepler's third law, years and AU

example.problem: Mars orbits in 1.881 years. How often is it at opposition, as seen from Earth?

M_{bol} = 4.74 − 2.5 log_{10}(L/L_{sun}).title: Absolute magnitude from luminosity
M_{bol} = 4.74 − 2.5 log_{10}(L/L_{sun}).about: A star's absolute bolometric magnitude from its luminosity in solar units, using the Sun's M_{bol} = 4.74. Each factor of 100 in luminosity is 5 magnitudes; brighter stars have smaller (more negative) magnitudes. Combine it with the distance modulus to get the apparent magnitude.
assumptions: Bolometric (all wavelengths); a filter band like V needs a bolometric correction

example.problem: A star is 100 times as luminous as the Sun. What is its absolute bolometric magnitude?
